title: Cost control: caching, model routing, batching, token accounting
story:
You cannot control what you cannot attribute, so the first piece of cost work is not a saving. It is recording, with every response, how many tokens went in and how many came out, which feature asked for them, and on whose behalf. Without that, every conversation about the bill is speculation, and speculation loses to whoever is most confident in the room.

Once you have the numbers, the shape of the bill is usually a surprise. Cost is charged on what you send and what you receive, so it is driven by the size of the input you assembled and the length of the output you permitted — not primarily by which model you chose. Teams reach for a cheaper model first because that is the visible knob, while the actual spend is the retrieved passages nobody has pruned and the instructions that grew for a year. Read your largest request before you shop for a discount.

With that established, four levers, roughly in the order they pay.

Send less. Everything in the input is paid for on every call, so the subtraction habit from context engineering is also the cheapest cost reduction available, and it usually improves quality at the same time because it removes what was competing with the evidence.

Reuse what repeats. Identical requests can return a stored answer. The embedding of a query you have seen before does not need computing again. And where the platform can reuse a stable prefix, the order you assemble things in becomes a cost decision as well as an attention one: fixed instructions at the front, variable content at the back, so the front can be reused rather than reprocessed.

Route by difficulty. Most requests do not need the most capable model, and the mix is usually lopsided — a small number of hard questions and a long tail of easy ones. Classify cheaply, send the easy ones somewhere cheap, and define what happens when the cheap path fails: escalate rather than degrade silently. Then measure quality per route against your case set, because a routing rule that quietly sends a third of your traffic to a model that handles it badly is a quality regression disguised as a saving.

Batch what nobody is waiting for. Embedding a corpus, enriching records, running evaluations — all of it belongs in a batch where throughput is what matters. Never batch something a person is sitting in front of, which is the one rule people break because the saving looks the same on a spreadsheet.

Then the thing that turns a bill into an incident, which deserves its own paragraph. A loop that calls a paid interface, with no cap, will keep going. Put a budget on every request, every user and every feature, decide in advance what happens at the limit, and make the limit a number in configuration rather than a habit of the people who wrote the code. The failure mode is not gradual: a retry loop and a bad case can spend a month's budget in an afternoon, and it does it at the exact moment nobody is watching.

Finally, the framing that keeps this honest. Every cost reduction is a quality risk, because all of them change what the system sees or which model answers. So each one is a change, and changes are run against the case set before and after. A cheaper system that answers worse is not a cheaper system — it is a different product, and it should be adopted knowingly if it is adopted at all.

problem.name: Attributing and bounding per-request spend
problem.shape: Every request costs money in proportion to what you send and what you allow back, and the total is invisible until it arrives.
tell: nobody can say which feature is responsible for most of the spend
a cheaper model is being discussed before anyone has read the largest request
a loop can call a paid interface with no cap
cost reductions have shipped without running the case set
problem.move: Record tokens in and out with the feature and the user on every response, then cut what you send, reuse what repeats, route easy work to cheap models with an explicit escalation, batch anything nobody is waiting for, and cap spend per request, user and feature.
problem.invariant: Spend is a function of the input you assembled and the output you permitted, so the size of the request is the first lever and the choice of model is not.
problem.breaks: Every reduction changes what the system sees or which model answers, so each one is a quality change and has to be measured as one.

cost.time: accounting and routing add work on every request, and the classifier on the routing path is itself a call
cost.space: caches and stored answers take room and need invalidation, which is its own small system
cost.beats: switching to a cheaper model, which is visible and often addresses the smaller term, and doing nothing, which prices the product by accident

worked.problem: Where does the money in one of these systems actually go, and what stops a bill becoming an incident?
worked.reasoning:
Into what you send and what you allow back, per call — which means the assembled input and the permitted output length, not primarily the choice of model.

So the first piece of work is not a saving at all, it is attribution: tokens in and tokens out recorded with every response, tagged with the feature and the user. Without that every discussion about the bill is speculation, and speculation loses to whoever is most confident.

Once I can see it, the order of levers is usually the reverse of what people reach for. Send less first, because everything in the input is paid on every call — the same subtraction that improves quality. Reuse what repeats: identical requests, embeddings of queries already seen, and where the platform allows a stable prefix to be reused, the assembly order becomes a cost decision too, with fixed instructions at the front and variable content at the back.

Then route by difficulty, because the mix is lopsided — a few hard questions and a long tail of easy ones — with an explicit escalation when the cheap path fails, and quality measured per route, or a routing rule becomes a quality regression disguised as a saving. And batch anything nobody is waiting for, while never batching something a person is sitting in front of.

What stops a bill becoming an incident is a cap, in configuration rather than in habit: per request, per user, per feature, with a defined behaviour at the limit. The failure is not gradual — a retry loop and one bad case can spend a month's budget in an afternoon, and it happens when nobody is watching.

And I would keep the framing honest. Every reduction changes what the system sees or who answers, so each is a change to be run against the case set. A cheaper system that answers worse is not cheaper, it is a different product.

problem.practice: Print your largest single request in full and read it end to end. Count what fraction of it is instructions that accumulated, examples that restate the instructions, and retrieved text that did not bear on the question. That fraction is your bill, and you will find more of it in one reading than in a month of comparing prices.

beats.broke: Spend is invisible per request, so it is discussed as a model-choice problem while the real driver is the input nobody has read and the loop nobody has capped.
beats.fix: Record tokens with the feature and the user, cut what you send, reuse what repeats, route easy work cheaply with explicit escalation, and batch anything offline.
beats.cost: Every reduction changes what the system sees or who answers, so all of them are quality changes that have to be measured against the case set.

interview.q: Where does the money in one of these systems actually go, and what stops a bill becoming an incident?
interview.trap: Starting with model price. The spend is dominated by the input you assembled and the output you allowed, so a cheaper model often addresses the smaller term while the largest request goes unread.
interview.answer:
Into what you send and what you allow back on every call, which means the assembled input and the permitted output length rather than the choice of model.

So the first task is attribution, not saving: tokens in and out on every response, tagged with feature and user. Without it, the cost conversation is speculation and the most confident person wins it.

The levers, in the order they usually pay: send less, since everything in the input is paid every call and the subtraction usually improves quality too; reuse what repeats, including a stable prefix, which makes assembly order a cost decision as well as an attention one; route by difficulty with an explicit escalation and per-route quality measurement, because a routing rule that sends a third of traffic to a model that handles it badly is a quality regression disguised as a saving; and batch whatever nobody is waiting for, while never batching something a person is watching.

What stops an incident is a cap in configuration rather than in habit — per request, per user, per feature, with defined behaviour at the limit. The failure is sudden: a retry loop and one bad case can spend a month's budget in an afternoon, while nobody is watching.

And every reduction is a quality change, so each one runs against the case set before and after. A cheaper system that answers worse is a different product, not a cheaper one.
